Define the target population and examine the sampling frame, recruitment, and inclusion probabilities. Weighting can help when selection differences are measured, but cannot guarantee correction for unknown gaps. A nonrandom sample can still support some questions; its limitations depend on the target inference.

examples.text: A city estimates all residents' transport habits by surveying people at downtown train stations during weekday mornings.
examples.note: The sampling locations and times exclude many travel patterns.

examples.text: A poll recruits only from a web panel, missing residents without reliable internet access.
examples.note: The frame systematically excludes part of the target population.

counters: Define the population and use a sampling frame that covers it as fully as possible.
Report recruitment and inclusion probabilities; compare sample composition with population data.
limitations: Sampling bias is not the same as low sample size, and some nonprobability samples can be informative for specific questions.
biases.evidenceNote: Survey and statistical methodology distinguishes selection in sampling from random sampling error and nonresponse.

biases.name: Selection bias
biases.summary: An estimate is distorted because cases enter, remain in, or are chosen for analysis according to factors related to the variables studied.
biases.body:
Selection bias is a broad family of distortions caused by how observations become part of an analysis. Conditioning on participation, survival, referral, or another selection factor can create or hide associations. It includes but is broader than biased initial sampling; even a representative starting sample can be distorted by later exclusions.

Map the full path from the target population to analyzed cases and identify what affects inclusion. Report exclusions and test how results change under plausible selection assumptions. Adjustment is not automatic: conditioning on the wrong variable can introduce rather than remove bias.

examples.text: A study of exercise and health includes only people who attend a clinic, where both illness and access to exercise affect attendance.
examples.note: Selection into the clinic can create a misleading relationship.

examples.text: A company analyzes only customers who renew, then concludes its service works well because dissatisfied customers have already left.
examples.note: Retention selects a favorable subset for analysis.

counters: Draw a causal diagram of inclusion and measure factors that affect selection.
Track exclusions and use design or sensitivity methods suited to the selection process.
limitations: Selection into a sample is not automatically bias if it does not distort the target estimate; define the estimand and mechanism.
biases.evidenceNote: Selection bias is a central causal-inference and epidemiologic concept, with multiple forms and no single correction.

biases.name: Selective perception
biases.summary: Expectations or interests can shape what information a person notices and how ambiguous evidence is interpreted.
biases.body:
Selective perception is preferential attention to information that fits current expectations, goals, or commitments. People may notice confirming details quickly while overlooking conflicting ones, or interpret ambiguous evidence in a favorable direction. This can happen without deliberate filtering.

Seek disconfirming observations and use a checklist that records evidence on both sides. Independent observers and explicit definitions help when judgments are consequential. Attention must be selective to function at all; the bias is an unbalanced selection that distorts the relevant conclusion.

examples.text: A coach notices every successful play that supports a favored strategy but attributes failures to player execution without reviewing the full record.
examples.note: The same strategy is interpreted asymmetrically across outcomes.

examples.text: A person worried about illness notices every minor symptom but discounts days when the symptom is absent.
examples.note: Expectation shapes which observations are attended to and remembered.

counters: Specify what evidence would count against the current view before reviewing new information.
Use complete logs or blinded evaluation rather than relying only on memory.
limitations: Selective attention is necessary and often useful; the label applies when the selection is systematically skewed relative to the task.
biases.evidenceNote: Selective perception is a broad term rather than one single mechanism; distinguish attention, interpretation, and memory effects.

biases.name: Self-consistency bias
biases.summary: Reconstructing one's past beliefs or actions as more consistent with the present self-image than they were.
biases.body:
Self-consistency bias smooths autobiographical memory so that earlier choices seem to fit who one believes oneself to be now. People may forget changes of view or reinterpret past motives as always aligned with current values. This can make personal history feel coherent while hiding learning, inconsistency, or genuine change.

Use dated records and ask what evidence or circumstances were different at the time. A coherent identity can be meaningful, but it should not be treated as an exact record. This label concerns remembered consistency; it differs from hindsight memory distortion, which specifically shifts a prior prediction toward a known outcome.

examples.text: A person who now supports remote work remembers having advocated for it years earlier, although old messages show they opposed it.
examples.note: The present position reshapes memory of the earlier belief.

examples.text: A manager recalls always having valued staff well-being, while past schedules show repeated choices that prioritized deadlines.
examples.note: Current self-image alters the account of prior behavior.

counters: Keep dated records of important decisions and reasons when later reflection matters.
Treat changed beliefs as evidence of learning rather than forcing a consistent story.
limitations: People can genuinely hold stable values over time; a perceived shift needs comparison with contemporaneous evidence.
biases.evidenceNote: Autobiographical memory is reconstructive; this label is broad and overlaps consistency motives and memory distortion.

biases.name: Self-serving bias
biases.summary: Explaining one's successes through personal qualities and failures through outside causes more than the evidence warrants.
biases.body:
Self-serving bias protects a favorable self-view through asymmetric attribution. A success may be credited to skill, while a failure is blamed on bad luck or unfair conditions. Such explanations can be accurate in particular cases; the bias appears when the standard shifts depending on whether the outcome flatters the self.

Compare explanations across both favorable and unfavorable outcomes and look for the same types of evidence. Include situational factors in both cases and personal contribution in both. Balanced attribution is not equal blame or credit; it means applying a consistent causal standard.

examples.text: A salesperson credits a strong quarter to their talent but blames a weak quarter entirely on the economy, without examining changes in effort or territory.
examples.note: Internal and external causes are selected according to whether the result is favorable.

examples.text: A student attributes a high grade to ability but a low grade to a biased examiner, without checking the marked work.
examples.note: The cause changes with the direction of the result.

counters: Review successes and failures using the same checklist of personal and situational causes.
Seek independent feedback and compare explanations with observable evidence.
limitations: Some successes and failures really do have different causes; asymmetry is not proof of bias without examining the cases.
biases.evidenceNote: Self-serving attribution is widely studied, but effects differ by culture, task, self-esteem, and outcome framing.

biases.name: Semmelweis reflex
biases.summary: Rejecting an unfamiliar claim reflexively because it conflicts with established beliefs or practice.
biases.body:
The Semmelweis reflex names a dismissive response to new evidence that challenges accepted practice. The idea is often invoked when institutions defend the status quo without seriously evaluating a proposal. It does not show that the rejected claim is correct: evidence can be weak, unsafe, or methodologically flawed.

Assess the evidence and the objections on their merits, using standards that apply to established and novel claims alike. A staged test can reduce risk while allowing a promising idea to be evaluated. The label comes from a popularized historical narrative and is sometimes used rhetorically, so it should not replace a precise account of why a proposal was rejected.

examples.text: A clinic dismisses a proposed infection-control procedure because “we have always done it this way,” without reviewing the supporting data.
examples.note: Tradition substitutes for evidence assessment.

examples.text: A team adopts an untested technique after critics are called reflexively conservative, without examining safety evidence.
examples.note: The label is used to bypass scrutiny in the opposite direction.

counters: Apply the same quality, safety, and replication standards to new and established practices.
State objections specifically and test claims in a controlled, proportionate way.
limitations: The phrase can be used to stigmatize legitimate criticism; rejection is not evidence of reflex or proof of an innovation's value.
biases.evidenceNote: The name refers to Ignaz Semmelweis, but accounts of the episode are historically simplified; use the label as a rhetorical description, not a complete history.

biases.name: Sexual overperception bias
biases.summary: Inferring sexual interest from another person's behavior more readily than their expressed intent or other evidence supports.
biases.body:
Sexual overperception bias describes a tendency to read ambiguous social cues as sexual interest. Friendliness, attention, or politeness can be interpreted as attraction, especially when the observer's own interest shapes the reading. The label concerns mistaken inference; it never overrides a person's direct statement about their boundaries or consent.

Treat ambiguous cues as ambiguous and rely on explicit, voluntary communication. Consider context and alternative explanations instead of inferring intent from friendliness. Findings about average differences between groups do not predict an individual's interest and should not be used to excuse unwanted behavior.

examples.text: A person interprets a colleague's warm conversation as sexual interest despite no invitation or statement of attraction.
examples.note: Friendly behavior is assigned a stronger meaning than it supports.

examples.text: Someone assumes a server is flirting because of attentive service, then ignores the server's clear attempt to end the interaction.
examples.note: Role-based politeness is mistaken for personal intent.

counters: Do not infer consent or sexual interest from ambiguous behavior; seek clear, freely given communication.
Accept a stated lack of interest without trying to reinterpret it.
limitations: Attraction can be expressed indirectly, but ambiguity is not permission and group averages do not establish an individual's intent.
biases.evidenceNote: The construct has been studied in social psychology, including sex-difference research; findings and interpretation remain context-sensitive.

biases.name: Shared-information bias
biases.summary: Groups often discuss information that everyone already knows more than equally important information held by only one member.
biases.body:
Shared-information bias occurs when common facts receive disproportionate airtime in group decisions, while unique information is not surfaced or integrated. Repeating familiar points feels safe and confirms agreement; members may assume others already know the details they alone possess. A group can therefore miss the evidence most likely to change its choice.

Collect individual information before discussion, invite each member to contribute unique facts, and explicitly search for information that could alter the ranking of options. Shared information is not unimportant; the problem is imbalance in discussion relative to what is decision-relevant.

examples.text: A hiring panel repeatedly discusses a candidate's résumé, known to all members, while one interviewer does not mention a reference check that raises a serious concern.
examples.note: Common details dominate while unique evidence remains unshared.

examples.text: A committee spends its meeting restating the proposal but never hears one member's data showing the expected cost is much higher.
examples.note: The unique information could change the decision but is not elicited.

counters: Ask each member to submit evidence independently before discussion.
Reserve time for unique facts and ask explicitly what could change the group's current favorite.
limitations: Unique information can be mistaken or irrelevant; the goal is to hear it and assess it, not automatically privilege it.
biases.evidenceNote: Group decision research has repeatedly studied hidden-profile tasks and the disproportionate discussion of shared information.

biases.name: Single-option aversion
biases.summary: An option can seem less attractive when presented alone because there is no comparison to clarify its value.
biases.body:
Single-option aversion describes reluctance to choose when only one option is visible. People may hesitate because they cannot judge whether the offering is good, whether alternatives exist, or whether choosing commits them prematurely. Adding a comparison can make the same option easier to evaluate.

Clarify the relevant criteria and whether a real alternative is needed before delaying a choice. More options can improve comparison but also add burden. The effect does not mean a person should choose an option that fails their needs simply because it is the only one shown.

examples.text: A customer declines a clearly suitable internet plan when it is the only plan shown but selects it when a more expensive plan is added for comparison.
examples.note: The comparison gives context to the same offer.

examples.text: A patient postpones choosing a standard treatment because the clinic presents it alone, although it meets the patient's stated priorities.
examples.note: Lack of comparison is mistaken for evidence that the option may be poor.

counters: State how the option meets the decision criteria and compare with a reasonable benchmark if useful.
Distinguish a true need for alternatives from discomfort caused only by a one-item display.
limitations: An isolated option may genuinely be inadequate or overpriced; comparison should inform judgment, not force acceptance.
biases.evidenceNote: The term appears in consumer choice research; findings depend on the decision, option quality, and comparison context.

biases.name: Social desirability bias
biases.summary: People may report attitudes or behavior in ways that appear socially approved rather than fully accurate.
biases.body:
Social desirability bias affects self-reports when respondents want to avoid judgment or present themselves favorably. They may underreport stigmatized actions and overreport approved ones. This can distort surveys and interviews even when respondents are not consciously trying to deceive.

Use confidential methods, neutral wording, and indirect measures when appropriate. Compare with behavioral data only when the comparison is valid and ethical. A socially desirable response may also reflect a genuine value, so the bias should not be presumed from any answer that sounds approved.

examples.text: Survey respondents report exercising more often than activity trackers indicate because regular exercise is viewed favorably.
examples.note: Self-presentation can shift reported frequency.

examples.text: People underreport alcohol use in a face-to-face interview but disclose more in a private anonymous questionnaire.
examples.note: Perceived judgment changes willingness to report.

counters: Protect anonymity and explain how responses will be used.
Use carefully validated indirect or behavioral measures for sensitive topics.
limitations: Behavioral measures can capture different constructs and have their own error; discrepancy alone does not establish deliberate misreporting.
biases.evidenceNote: Social desirability is a recognized survey-method issue; its impact varies with topic, culture, and administration mode.

biases.name: Social projection
biases.summary: Estimating what others think or do by using one's own attitudes or characteristics as a stand-in.
biases.body:
Social projection is the use of one's own preferences, beliefs, or behavior as a guide to what other people are like. It can be an efficient guess when people share relevant circumstances, but it becomes biased when personal experience is unrepresentative. Projection can create false consensus and make disagreement seem unusual.

Ask people directly or use representative evidence when their preferences matter. Distinguish a prediction based on shared context from an assumption based only on the self. This term overlaps illusory self–other similarity, but projection emphasizes the estimation process rather than the resulting perception of similarity.

examples.text: A manager who prefers email assumes the whole team wants written updates and removes weekly check-ins without asking.
examples.note: Personal communication preference is projected onto coworkers.

examples.text: A person who enjoys political debate assumes their friends welcome being challenged in casual conversation.
examples.note: One's own comfort is used to estimate others' reactions.

counters: Collect preferences from the people affected rather than relying on personal intuition.
Use a representative sample when estimating a group's views.
limitations: Projection can be accurate when people genuinely share circumstances; test rather than assume either similarity or difference.
biases.evidenceNote: Social projection is a broad social-cognitive process studied across attitudes, relationships, and group judgment.

biases.name: Social selection bias
biases.summary: Inferring a broad social pattern from people encountered through a network or participation process that selects who is visible.
biases.body:
Social-selection bias arises when contacts, friends, or participants are treated as a representative cross-section despite being selected through social ties or access. People tend to meet others with shared settings, interests, and resources, so observed behavior may not characterize the wider population. The problem can affect informal judgments as well as formal studies.

Identify how people entered the network and who is absent. Compare claims with a sample that matches the population of interest. Social networks can provide useful local knowledge, but their composition should not be mistaken for a population estimate.

examples.text: A city official estimates residents' views from meetings attended mostly by homeowners with flexible work schedules.
examples.note: The participation route makes some residents more visible than others.

examples.text: A person assumes most young adults own homes because nearly all people in their professional circle do.
examples.note: A selected social network is not a representative sample.

counters: Describe the social and recruitment process that produced the observed contacts.
Use population surveys or multiple recruitment routes to include less visible groups.
limitations: A selected group can answer questions about itself; the concern is generalizing beyond its membership without evidence.
biases.evidenceNote: The label overlaps selection and network sampling concepts; specify whether the claim concerns casual inference or a formal study.

biases.name: Source-monitoring error
biases.summary: Remembering information while confusing whether it was perceived, imagined, inferred, or learned from another source.
biases.body:
A source-monitoring error occurs when a person recalls content but misidentifies its origin. Familiar details from imagination, conversation, media, or direct perception can become difficult to distinguish, especially over time. This can cause a report to sound firsthand when the information came from elsewhere.

Ask how and when each detail was encountered, and preserve original records for consequential claims. Source cues such as context and sensory detail can help but are imperfect. This concept overlaps misattribution of memory; use source-monitoring error when the source decision itself is the focus.

examples.text: A person remembers a childhood story told by a parent as something they personally witnessed.
examples.note: The remembered content is assigned to firsthand experience.

examples.text: A witness sees a suspect's picture in a news report and later feels certain they saw that person at the original event.
examples.note: A later source is confused with event perception.

counters: Record where information came from when it is first encountered.
In interviews, ask for source details without suggesting a preferred answer.
limitations: A source-monitoring error does not prove the content itself is false; independent evidence may confirm it.
biases.evidenceNote: Source monitoring is a well-developed area of memory research; errors vary with delay, familiarity, and source similarity.

biases.name: Spectrum bias
biases.summary: A diagnostic test's measured accuracy can change when the patients studied differ in disease severity or alternative conditions from those who will use it.
biases.body:
Spectrum bias occurs when diagnostic accuracy is estimated from a patient mix unlike the intended population. A test may distinguish severe disease from healthy controls but perform less well among people with mild disease or similar conditions. Sensitivity and specificity measured in a narrow sample may therefore not transfer to routine care.

Evaluate a test in the setting and patient spectrum where it will be used, including relevant alternatives and disease stages. Report who was enrolled and why. A difference in accuracy can also reflect prevalence or methods, so those factors should be separated rather than attributed automatically to spectrum.

examples.text: A blood test is evaluated on patients with advanced disease and exceptionally healthy volunteers, then promoted for screening people with mild symptoms.
examples.note: The study groups create an easier diagnostic contrast than real practice.

examples.text: A radiology algorithm is tested at one specialist hospital with a narrow patient mix and then used in community clinics serving broader conditions.
examples.note: Case spectrum and setting differ from intended use.

counters: Recruit a representative range of disease severity and alternative diagnoses.
Validate accuracy prospectively in the intended clinical setting.
limitations: Accuracy can vary for reasons beyond spectrum, including thresholds and verification methods; study context must be reported.
biases.evidenceNote: Spectrum effects are central in diagnostic-test methodology and can coexist with referral and verification bias.

biases.name: Spotlight effect
biases.summary: Overestimating how much other people notice one's appearance, actions, or mistakes.
biases.body:
The spotlight effect occurs because one's own experience is highly accessible, making it seem more visible to everyone else. People may assume others noticed a stain, awkward remark, or small error when observers were focused on themselves or other tasks. The effect can increase embarrassment and self-consciousness.

Use direct feedback or evidence about what others actually noticed rather than estimating from the intensity of one's own feeling. Other people sometimes do notice, especially in attention-focused settings; the bias is overestimating attention, not believing one is never observed.

examples.text: A student thinks the whole lecture hall noticed a small stain on their shirt, though classmates later cannot recall it.
examples.note: Personal salience is mistaken for audience attention.

examples.text: A speaker believes one brief stumble ruined a presentation, while listeners remember the main argument.
examples.note: The speaker's error feels more prominent from the inside.

counters: Ask what observers actually recall rather than inferring from personal embarrassment.
Shift attention to the task and audience instead of monitoring every personal cue.
limitations: Visible or unusual behavior can attract attention; the effect is about overestimating its degree or duration.
biases.evidenceNote: The spotlight effect was demonstrated in social psychology experiments involving conspicuous clothing and performance.

biases.name: Status quo bias
biases.summary: Preferring the existing arrangement beyond what its actual benefits, switching costs, and risks justify.
biases.body:
Status quo bias is an undue preference for the current option. Defaults, ownership, familiarity, and anticipated regret can make change feel riskier than keeping things as they are. Inaction is still a choice and can carry costs, even when those costs are less visible.

Compare the current arrangement with alternatives using the same criteria, including switching costs and consequences of delay. A stable choice can be sensible when change is costly or evidence favors the current state. The bias is not simply preferring continuity; it is allowing the default to receive an unjustified advantage.

examples.text: A household stays on an expensive energy plan for years because switching requires a short comparison and signup process.
examples.note: Default and friction outweigh the ongoing cost without deliberate review.

examples.text: An organization keeps an outdated approval process because staff already know it, despite repeated delays and no review of alternatives.
examples.note: Familiarity receives more weight than actual performance.

counters: Review the current option as if selecting it anew and compare it with alternatives.
Make switching costs and the cost of staying explicit; set periodic review dates.
limitations: Switching can introduce real costs or risks; retaining the status quo may be the best-supported choice.
biases.evidenceNote: Status quo bias is studied in choice, policy defaults, and behavioral economics; it overlaps endowment and loss-aversion effects.

biases.name: Stereotypical memory bias
biases.summary: Reconstructing or recalling a person or event in ways that fit a group stereotype.
biases.body:
Stereotypical memory bias occurs when expectations about a group shape which details are retained or later reconstructed. A person may remember stereotype-consistent behavior more readily, or misremember an ambiguous detail to fit an expectation. The result can strengthen a group belief even when the original event was more varied.

Separate observed details from interpretation, and check records or independent accounts where accuracy matters. Ask whether the same behavior would be remembered differently if the person's group were different. Stereotypes can influence memory without making every recalled detail false.

examples.text: After meeting a quiet accountant, someone later recalls them as especially cautious because that trait fits a stereotype about the profession.
examples.note: Expectation shapes the remembered degree of a trait.

examples.text: A witness remembers a person from a stigmatized group as carrying an object associated with a crime, though the original report was uncertain.
examples.note: Stereotypic expectation can sharpen an ambiguous memory.

counters: Record observations promptly and distinguish direct details from inferences.
Use independent records and blind review when group expectations could affect recall.
limitations: A remembered trait may be accurate; the bias concerns systematic stereotype-consistent distortion, not all group-related memory.
biases.evidenceNote: Social cognition research finds stereotype effects on memory under some conditions; results depend on ambiguity and task.

biases.name: Stereotyping
biases.summary: Using a generalized belief about a group as a substitute for adequate evidence about an individual.
biases.body:
Stereotyping applies a perceived group pattern to a particular person without enough individual evidence. Even a statistically accurate group average may poorly predict an individual and can lead to unfair treatment when used as a shortcut. Stereotypes can be positive or negative, and can shape expectations before behavior is observed.

Evaluate people on relevant individual evidence and question whether group information is valid, necessary, and fair for the decision. Avoid treating a category as a complete description. This does not mean group-level data are never useful; it means they cannot automatically replace personal assessment.

examples.text: A recruiter assumes an older applicant will struggle with new software without asking about their actual experience.
examples.note: An age-based expectation substitutes for individual evidence.

examples.text: A teacher expects a student from a high-performing neighborhood to need no support and overlooks clear signs of difficulty.
examples.note: A seemingly favorable stereotype can still misjudge an individual.

counters: Use job- or task-relevant criteria and gather evidence about the individual.
Check whether category information is necessary, valid, and being applied consistently.
limitations: Group statistics can be relevant for population-level planning; their use for an individual decision requires careful justification.
biases.evidenceNote: Stereotyping is a broad social-cognitive process with varied definitions; distinguish belief, application, and discriminatory action.

biases.name: Subadditivity effect
biases.summary: Judged probabilities for separate parts of an event can sum to more than the probability assigned to the whole event.
biases.body:
The subadditivity effect occurs when people assign probabilities to component outcomes that together exceed their estimate for the broader event containing them. Breaking a category into vivid subcases can make each easier to imagine and increase its judged likelihood. A mathematically coherent probability model requires mutually exclusive components to sum to the total.

Define events precisely, ensure categories do not overlap, and check that probabilities add consistently. Decomposition can improve estimation when it reveals neglected possibilities, but it can also inflate totals through inconsistent judgments. The effect concerns subjective estimates, not a mathematical property of actual probabilities.

examples.text: A forecaster estimates separate chances for several types of transport delay that sum to 70%, but assigns only 50% to “any delay.”
examples.note: The component estimates conflict with the encompassing event estimate.

examples.text: A person judges the risk of several named illnesses individually as higher in total than the chance of being ill at all.
examples.note: Unpacked categories draw more attention than the broader event.

counters: Use a probability tree or mutually exclusive categories and verify totals against the parent event.
Calibrate estimates against observed frequencies and avoid double-counting overlapping outcomes.
limitations: Subadditivity of human judgments is not the same as subadditive measures in mathematics; event definitions and overlap must be checked.
biases.evidenceNote: Subadditivity has been examined in probability judgment and forecasting research, including category unpacking.

biases.name: Subjective validation
biases.summary: Treating a claim as especially credible because it feels personally accurate, despite lacking evidence that distinguishes it from alternatives.
biases.body:
Subjective validation occurs when a person sees personal meaning or fit as evidence that a broad claim is uniquely true. General descriptions can match many people because readers supply their own examples and overlook mismatches. The feeling of recognition can be sincere while the claim remains weakly tested.

Ask whether the description would also feel accurate to people with different traits, and specify predictions that could prove it wrong. Independent evidence matters more than emotional resonance when evaluating factual claims. Personal meaning can still matter for reflection or art, where empirical accuracy is not the only goal.

examples.text: A person reads a vague personality profile saying they “sometimes enjoy company but need time alone” and treats it as precise evidence of a special type.
examples.note: A broad description fits many people and invites selective matching.

examples.text: A horoscope feels accurate because a reader connects its general warning to a recent personal setback.
examples.note: The reader's own interpretation supplies the apparent specificity.

counters: Look for specific, testable claims and consider how often they would fit people generally.
Compare predictions with independent outcomes rather than relying on a sense of personal fit.
limitations: A statement can be meaningful without being a verified factual account; subjective value and empirical support are different questions.
biases.evidenceNote: The concept overlaps the Barnum/Forer effect and confirmation processes; terminology varies across fields.

biases.name: Suggestibility
biases.summary: A person's memory, judgment, or report can be influenced by information or cues supplied by another person.
biases.body:
Suggestibility is responsiveness to suggestion, including leading questions, expectations, or implied answers. Suggested details can affect what a person reports, particularly when the original memory is uncertain, but influence does not mean the person is deliberately deceptive. The term is broad and can refer to memory or other judgments.

Use open-ended prompts, avoid introducing details before an initial account, and keep track of what information was supplied. Independent corroboration is important when the report has serious consequences. Suggestions can sometimes help retrieve accurate information, so the content still needs evaluation rather than automatic rejection.

examples.text: A child asked repeatedly whether a visitor took a toy begins to report seeing the visitor take it despite initially saying they did not know.
examples.note: Question repetition implies an expected answer and can shape the report.

examples.text: A witness is told that other people saw a weapon and later incorporates a weapon into an uncertain memory.
examples.note: Information from others can influence later recall.

counters: Use neutral, open-ended questions and document the interview sequence.
Separate spontaneous recall from details introduced by the interviewer or other witnesses.
limitations: Suggestion effects vary with age, context, memory strength, and questioning; a suggested detail is not automatically false.
biases.evidenceNote: Suggestibility is studied in memory and interview research; it is broader than the misinformation effect.

biases.name: Surrogation
biases.summary: Treating a measure used to represent an objective as if improving the measure were the objective itself.
biases.body:
Surrogation happens when a proxy or performance metric replaces the real goal in people's decisions. A measure may start as a convenient indicator, then attract effort because it is counted, even when optimizing it no longer improves the outcome it was meant to represent. This resembles Goodhart's law, though the terms are not identical.

Keep the underlying objective explicit and check whether the metric still tracks it as incentives change. Use multiple indicators and qualitative review where appropriate. Metrics can coordinate work and reveal progress; the risk is assuming that a rising proxy necessarily means the real objective is being met.

examples.text: A call center rewards staff for short calls, leading them to end conversations quickly while customer problems remain unresolved.
examples.note: Call length becomes the target instead of successful assistance.

examples.text: A school focuses on test scores as the measure of learning, narrowing instruction to tested items while students struggle to apply knowledge.
examples.note: The indicator displaces the broader educational objective.

counters: Pair proxy metrics with direct measures of the underlying outcome and check for unintended responses.
Review incentives periodically and revise measures when they stop tracking the goal.
limitations: A metric is not inherently a surrogate failure; it can be useful if its relationship to the objective remains valid.
biases.evidenceNote: Surrogation is used in management-control research; its relation to target substitution and Goodhart effects varies by field.

biases.name: Survivorship bias
biases.summary: Drawing conclusions from cases that remain visible while overlooking relevant cases that failed, disappeared, or were excluded.
biases.body:
Survivorship bias arises when analysis focuses on entities that lasted long enough to be observed and omits those that failed or exited. Survivors often have different histories from the full set, so their traits can appear more successful or necessary than they were. The missing cases may be hard to find precisely because they did not survive.

Define the original cohort and include failures, exits, and losses where possible. Compare outcomes from the full population rather than selecting only visible examples. Survivors can still teach useful lessons, but their stories alone cannot establish what predicts success.

examples.text: An investor studies only funds that still operate and concludes their strategy reliably beats the market, omitting funds that closed after poor performance.
examples.note: Failed funds disappear from the comparison set.

examples.text: A writer copies habits of famous entrepreneurs without considering how many people used the same habits and failed.
examples.note: Visible success stories omit the less visible failures.

counters: Identify the original population and track closures, dropouts, and other missing cases.
Compare successful and failed cases using consistent definitions and time periods.
limitations: Survivor case studies can generate hypotheses; the bias concerns treating them as representative evidence of success rates or causes.
biases.evidenceNote: Survivorship bias is a standard concern in finance, history, and performance analysis.

biases.name: System justification
biases.summary: Motivations to see existing social arrangements as legitimate can shape judgments, including among people disadvantaged by them.
biases.body:
System justification is the tendency or motive to defend existing institutions and social arrangements as fair, natural, or necessary. Doing so can reduce uncertainty and preserve a sense of order, but may also lead people to rationalize inequalities or oppose changes that could benefit them. The concept is a social-psychological theory, not proof that every defense of an institution is biased.

Examine how an arrangement works, who benefits, who bears costs, and what alternatives exist. Separate stability or familiarity from evidence of fairness and effectiveness. People can defend a system for informed reasons; the label requires examining the judgment process, not simply whether someone supports the status quo.

examples.text: Workers facing unequal pay explain the gap as deserved because they assume the organization rewards merit fairly, without reviewing pay criteria.
examples.note: Belief in institutional fairness can protect the legitimacy of an unequal arrangement.

examples.text: A citizen opposes a reform that would expand their access because they regard the current allocation as naturally deserved.
examples.note: Existing rules are treated as legitimate without considering alternatives.

counters: Compare stated principles with how outcomes and opportunities are actually distributed.
Include affected groups' evidence and assess feasible alternatives rather than equating stability with fairness.
limitations: Institutional arrangements can be legitimate or effective; support alone is not evidence of system-justifying bias.
biases.evidenceNote: System justification is a social-psychological theory associated with Jost and colleagues; its scope and mechanisms are debated.

biases.name: Telescoping effect
biases.summary: Remembering an event as closer to or farther from the present than it actually occurred.
biases.body:
The telescoping effect is temporal displacement in memory. Forward telescoping places an older event too recently; backward telescoping places a recent event too far in the past. This can make events seem to fall inside or outside a survey's reporting window and distort estimates of frequency.

Use calendars, receipts, medical records, or other dated anchors when timing matters. Ask about distinctive landmarks rather than relying on an overall sense of when something happened. The effect concerns remembered timing and is different from simply forgetting the event.

examples.text: A survey respondent reports a repair from last year as having happened in the past month, inflating the recent repair count.
examples.note: An older event is moved forward into the survey period.

examples.text: A patient remembers a recent symptom episode as occurring much earlier, making the interval appear longer than it was.
examples.note: A recent event is displaced backward in time.

counters: Use dated records and clear reference periods for event histories.
Anchor recall to holidays, appointments, or other verifiable milestones.
limitations: The direction and magnitude vary with event salience, repetition, and survey design; timing records may also be incomplete.
biases.evidenceNote: Survey research distinguishes forward and backward telescoping as sources of reporting error.

biases.name: Third-person effect
biases.summary: Expecting media messages to influence other people more than oneself, sometimes with consequences for regulation or behavior.
biases.body:
The third-person effect is a perceived gap in media influence: people often judge others as more susceptible to persuasive or harmful content than themselves. The judgment can shape support for restrictions, education, or censorship. It does not establish that media actually affect everyone equally, nor that no one is personally influenced.

Ask respondents to estimate influence on themselves and comparable others using the same measure, and distinguish perceived effects from observed behavior. People can accurately recognize different vulnerabilities, so the size and direction of the gap should be measured rather than assumed.

examples.text: A viewer says online misinformation is dangerous for other users but believes their own opinions are unaffected by the same posts.
examples.note: The observer places themselves outside the likely audience effect.

examples.text: A parent supports restricting a program for teenagers while assuming their own media choices are not shaped by advertising.
examples.note: Perceived vulnerability is assigned asymmetrically.

counters: Measure perceived influence on self and others separately, with matched questions.
Use behavioral evidence when evaluating actual effects and avoid assuming personal immunity.
limitations: People can differ in exposure and susceptibility; perceived asymmetry may be accurate in some circumstances.
biases.evidenceNote: The effect is widely studied in communication research; perceived and actual media effects are distinct measures.

biases.name: Time-saving bias
biases.summary: Misjudging how much travel time changes when speed changes, often because time is inversely related to speed.
biases.body:
Time-saving bias is a predictable error in estimating travel-time reductions from speed increases. Since time equals distance divided by speed, the same increase in speed saves more time at low speeds than at high speeds. People often underestimate the benefit of raising a low speed and overestimate the benefit of raising a high one.

Calculate the time difference using the actual distance and speeds rather than treating speed changes as linear. Include stops, congestion, and safety constraints when estimating a real trip. The mathematical relation applies to constant speeds over a fixed distance; ordinary travel conditions may change at the same time.

examples.text: A driver expects raising speed from 30 to 40 km/h to save less time than raising it from 100 to 110 km/h over the same distance.
examples.note: The time saved is actually greater for the lower-speed increase, assuming fixed distance and constant speed.

examples.text: A commuter believes driving 10 km/h faster on a highway will substantially shorten a trip but does not account for lights and congestion.
examples.note: The theoretical speed difference is not the whole journey time.

counters: Use distance divided by speed to calculate ideal travel times at each speed.
Then add realistic stops and congestion and consider safety and legal limits.
limitations: The simple calculation assumes constant speed and fixed distance; route and traffic changes can dominate actual savings.
biases.evidenceNote: The speed-time relation is mathematical; observed estimation bias is documented in travel judgment studies.

biases.name: Trait-ascription bias
biases.summary: Explaining one's own behavior through changing situations while treating other people's behavior as evidence of stable traits.
biases.body:
Trait-ascription bias is an asymmetry in how behavior is explained. People know the situational details behind their own actions, while observing others from the outside; they may therefore see their own behavior as flexible and another person's as revealing a fixed character. This is related to, but not identical with, the fundamental attribution error.

Consider situational evidence for others as readily as for oneself, and look for repeated behavior across contexts before inferring a stable trait. Personality can predict behavior, but one episode rarely establishes a person's character. The bias is a comparative tendency, not a rule that trait judgments are always wrong.

examples.text: A manager explains their own missed deadline by a late dependency but labels an employee who misses one as unreliable.
examples.note: Situation is used for self and disposition for another person.

examples.text: A driver says their own speeding was caused by an emergency but calls another speeding driver reckless without knowing the context.
examples.note: Private situational information produces different standards.

counters: Ask what situational constraints applied to both people before assigning traits.
Base stable character judgments on patterns across situations, not isolated acts.
limitations: Stable traits can matter and situations may not excuse harmful conduct; the task is consistent causal evaluation.
biases.evidenceNote: Related attribution asymmetries have distinct definitions in social psychology; this label is used variably.

biases.name: Truth bias
biases.summary: A default tendency to treat communication as truthful, which can persist even when reasons for doubt deserve attention.
biases.body:
Truth bias is the tendency to accept messages as truthful unless there is reason to question them. Everyday communication would be costly if every statement required full verification, so a provisional default can be functional. It becomes an error when acceptance continues despite contradictions, incentives to deceive, or evidence that calls for checking.

Match verification effort to stakes and available evidence. Check claims independently when consequences are significant, while avoiding blanket suspicion that makes ordinary conversation impossible. This differs from the illusory truth effect: repetition can increase perceived truth, while truth bias concerns the baseline tendency to believe a speaker.

examples.text: A buyer accepts a seller's claim about a used car's accident history without checking records, despite inconsistent service documents.
examples.note: Default trust persists when there are specific reasons to verify.

examples.text: A manager treats a confident verbal report as accurate even after independent data show conflicting results.
examples.note: Speaker credibility substitutes for checking evidence.

counters: Use proportionate verification based on stakes, inconsistency, and the speaker's access to evidence.
Distinguish a speaker's sincerity from whether the claim is factually correct.
limitations: Initial trust is often efficient and socially necessary; the concern is failing to update when evidence warrants doubt.
biases.evidenceNote: Truth bias is studied in deception-detection research; people are often poor lie detectors, but the default is not universal.

biases.name: Ultimate attribution error
biases.summary: Explaining out-group members' bad behavior as dispositional and their good behavior as situational, while applying the reverse pattern to one's own group.
biases.body:
The ultimate attribution error extends attribution asymmetry across groups. Unfavorable actions by an out-group may be treated as proof of its character, while favorable actions are explained away as exceptions or circumstances. For one's own group, the explanation may reverse. This pattern can preserve stereotypes despite contrary examples.

Compare explanations for similar acts across groups and look for evidence of repeated patterns rather than dismissing counterexamples selectively. Context matters for every actor. The label does not imply that all group differences are imagined; it identifies uneven standards in causal interpretation.

examples.text: A commentator calls an out-group protester's violence proof that the group is violent but calls an in-group protester's similar act an isolated lapse.
examples.note: The same conduct is generalized differently by group membership.

examples.text: A manager credits a favored team's success to ability but explains a rival team's success as an easy assignment.
examples.note: Positive evidence is attributed asymmetrically.

counters: Use matched comparisons and the same standards for dispositional and situational explanations.
Track how counterexamples are handled for each group rather than discounting them automatically.
limitations: Groups may face different conditions; attribution bias requires showing that explanations shift beyond what those differences support.
biases.evidenceNote: The concept is rooted in social attribution research and is related to intergroup attribution bias.

biases.name: Uniqueness bias
biases.summary: Overestimating how unusual one's situation, ability, or problem is compared with relevantly similar cases.
biases.body:
Uniqueness bias is the belief that one's circumstances are unusually distinctive, which can discourage use of base rates or advice from comparable cases. People may underreport common difficulties or assume their own situation cannot be helped by ordinary solutions. The label is broad and may refer to false uniqueness in social comparison.

Define the reference class carefully and identify what is genuinely distinctive before rejecting comparisons. Similar cases can offer useful starting points without erasing individual differences. A person's situation may be unusual; the bias is assuming uniqueness without checking.

examples.text: A new parent assumes no one else has experienced their exhaustion and avoids a support group that could help.
examples.note: A common difficulty is treated as uniquely personal.

examples.text: A founder dismisses industry failure rates because their company is “different,” without specifying how its conditions differ.
examples.note: A claim of uniqueness shields a forecast from comparison.

counters: Search for a relevant reference class and state the features that make the case similar or different.
Use base rates as a starting point, then adjust for evidence-based differences.
limitations: Overgeneralizing from reference cases can also mislead; genuine individual differences should be assessed, not erased.
biases.evidenceNote: The label overlaps false uniqueness and uniqueness-seeking constructs; usage is not fully standardized.

biases.name: Unit bias
biases.summary: Treating one package, serving, or other presented unit as the appropriate amount even when unit sizes differ arbitrarily.
biases.body:
Unit bias is the tendency to use a presented unit as a cue for the proper amount. A single package or serving can feel like one natural portion, so people may consume more when the unit is larger without corresponding need. The size of a unit is often set by packaging or convention, not by a person's requirements.

Check quantities and serving sizes independently of package boundaries. Smaller portions or visible measurement can help when intake matters. A unit can be a useful guide, but its appropriateness depends on the task and person.

examples.text: A person eats an entire large bag of snacks because it counts as one package, though a smaller bowl would have been enough.
examples.note: Package size becomes the stopping rule.

examples.text: A diner finishes an oversized restaurant portion because it is one serving on the plate, regardless of hunger.
examples.note: Presented unit defines the amount consumed.

counters: Use measured portions or personal need rather than package size as the default amount.
Make unit quantities visible and compare them with relevant recommendations or goals.
limitations: One unit can be a practical and suitable amount; the bias concerns arbitrary unit size controlling behavior.
biases.evidenceNote: Unit bias is studied in consumption and portion-size research; effects depend on product, context, and individual needs.

biases.name: Verification bias
biases.summary: Diagnostic accuracy estimates can be distorted when confirmatory testing is more likely for some initial test results or patient groups.
biases.body:
Verification bias occurs when the reference standard used to confirm disease is not applied equally to everyone. If mainly people with a positive initial test receive definitive testing, false negatives may go undetected and accuracy estimates become distorted. Verification can also depend on symptoms or other factors, complicating comparisons.

Apply the reference procedure to all participants when feasible, or use designs and statistical methods that account for differential verification. Report who received confirmation and why. This differs from spectrum bias, which concerns the patient mix; both can occur in the same diagnostic study.

examples.text: A study sends only patients with a positive screening result for biopsy, then counts nearly all verified positives as true cases.
examples.note: Unverified negative results may conceal false negatives.

examples.text: Doctors order a gold-standard scan mainly for patients whose initial test and symptoms agree, leaving discordant cases unconfirmed.
examples.note: Verification probability depends on information related to disease status.

counters: Verify all participants with the same reference standard where ethical and practical.
Document verification patterns and use appropriate correction methods when testing is selective.
limitations: Reference standards may be invasive or costly, making universal verification impractical; conclusions then depend on design assumptions.
biases.evidenceNote: Verification bias is a recognized diagnostic-study risk, also called work-up bias in some contexts.

biases.name: Volunteer bias
biases.summary: People who volunteer for a study differ relevantly from those who do not, limiting the representativeness of findings.
biases.body:
Volunteer bias is a form of selection in which willingness to participate is related to traits or outcomes under study. Volunteers may have more time, stronger opinions, greater health interest, or more confidence than nonvolunteers. Findings can therefore misrepresent prevalence or behavior in the wider population.

Describe how participants were recruited and compare them with the target population. Use broader recruitment or follow-up where feasible. Volunteer samples can still be useful for testing a mechanism or studying a defined group; the limitation concerns how far results generalize.

examples.text: A university wellness study recruits from a health fair, attracting people more interested in health than the average student.
examples.note: The volunteering channel selects for the study's topic.

examples.text: A survey of workplace morale is completed mainly by workers with very positive or very negative views, while neutral employees ignore it.
examples.note: Opinion strength affects willingness to volunteer.

counters: Recruit through multiple channels and compare volunteers with eligible nonparticipants.
Report participation rates and assess how plausible volunteer differences affect conclusions.
limitations: A volunteer sample is not automatically unsuitable; it may answer questions limited to the people who volunteered.
biases.evidenceNote: Volunteer bias is a standard selection concern in psychology and health studies and overlaps participation bias.

biases.name: Well-traveled-road effect
biases.summary: People may judge familiar routes or tasks as taking less time than comparable unfamiliar ones.
biases.body:
The well-traveled-road effect is a difference in perceived duration for familiar and unfamiliar journeys or tasks. Familiarity may reduce attention to elapsed time or make the route easier to anticipate, causing a routine trip to feel shorter. Actual travel time can also differ because of route conditions, so subjective estimates should be separated from clock time.

Compare matched distances and conditions using measured duration as well as perceived duration. For planning, use time records rather than familiarity alone. The label concerns judgment, not an assertion that every familiar trip is objectively faster.

examples.text: A commuter estimates a familiar 40-minute drive as “about half an hour” but accurately remembers the duration of a new route.
examples.note: Familiarity changes the perceived passage of time.

examples.text: A worker underestimates a routine monthly report because the steps feel effortless, though logs show it takes as long as a new report.
examples.note: Task familiarity can influence duration judgment.

counters: Track elapsed time for familiar and unfamiliar cases rather than relying on impressions.
Use comparable routes or tasks and account for traffic, interruptions, and task complexity.
limitations: Familiarity can genuinely improve efficiency; perceived and objective duration must be measured separately.
biases.evidenceNote: The effect is reported in travel-time estimation research; it is distinct from the planning fallacy, though they can overlap.

biases.name: Zero-risk bias
biases.summary: Preferring to eliminate one risk entirely over a larger reduction in total harm when complete elimination feels especially reassuring.
biases.body:
Zero-risk bias is a preference for removing a risk to zero rather than making a larger overall reduction across risks. The certainty of eliminating one hazard can feel more satisfying than reducing a larger hazard substantially, even when the latter prevents more expected harm. The choice can still be reasonable if the eliminated risk has special moral or practical importance.

Compare absolute risk reductions, affected people, severity, and costs. Ask whether a zero target is a real requirement or mainly attractive because it sounds complete. Risk cannot always be reduced to a single expected-value calculation, but the trade-off should be explicit.

examples.text: A city spends heavily to eliminate a tiny playground hazard while declining a cheaper measure that would substantially reduce traffic injuries nearby.
examples.note: Certainty about one risk displaces a larger reduction in total harm.

examples.text: A manager removes a low-probability software risk entirely while ignoring a common failure mode that could be reduced across all users.
examples.note: Zero on one dimension is valued over broader risk reduction.

counters: Compare expected harms and cost-effectiveness across all available controls.
State any legitimate zero-risk requirement, such as a legal or ethical threshold, before ranking options.
limitations: Complete elimination can be justified when even a small risk is unacceptable or inequitable; the label does not make zero-risk policies irrational.
biases.evidenceNote: Zero-risk preference is documented in decision research, including environmental and health-risk choices.

biases.name: Zero-sum bias
biases.summary: Assuming that one person's gain must equal another's loss even when cooperation or exchange could increase total value.
biases.body:
Zero-sum bias treats a situation as a fixed pie when the total can grow. This assumption can frame cooperation as surrender and intensify competition, even where trade, coordination, or innovation creates mutual benefit. Some resources really are scarce and rivalrous, so the structure of the situation matters.

Identify whether the resource is fixed, whether parties value parts differently, and whether cooperation can create additional value. Negotiation should distinguish distributive questions about dividing a surplus from integrative opportunities to expand it. The label is not a claim that every conflict can be solved with win-win outcomes.

examples.text: Two departments refuse to share a specialist, assuming any support to the other team reduces their own output, though a joint schedule could raise both teams' results.
examples.note: Coordination could expand total capacity rather than divide a fixed amount.

examples.text: A negotiator rejects a trade in which each side gives up something it values less for something it values more.
examples.note: Different priorities can create mutual gains.

counters: Check whether cooperation, substitution, or different valuations can expand the available benefit.
Separate the size of the total surplus from how it will be divided.
limitations: Many goods are genuinely scarce and rivalrous; a zero-sum analysis can be accurate for a fixed resource under fixed rules.
biases.evidenceNote: The label is used in social judgment and negotiation research; application depends on whether the underlying resource is fixed.
